definition: A power distribution network is the interconnected source, conductors, planes, vias, capacitors, and loads that deliver power across a circuit.
Target impedance is the maximum desired PDN impedance derived from an allowed voltage deviation divided by a specified load-current step.
Voltage ripple is the allowed or measured variation of a power rail around its intended level over a specified condition or bandwidth.
A load step is a specified change in current demand used to evaluate power-delivery response.
Analysis bandwidth is the frequency range over which a requirement or simulation result is intended to apply.
Decoupling is the use of local energy storage and controlled connection impedance to reduce supply disturbances seen by a circuit load.
A decoupling capacitor is a capacitor placed and selected to help provide local transient current and reduce power-rail impedance over a useful frequency range.
Equivalent series resistance models the resistive loss associated with a real capacitor or other reactive component.
Equivalent series inductance models the inductive behavior introduced by a real capacitor, package, and connection structure.
Connection distance is the physical separation between a required decoupling component and its target connection as constrained by the design rule.
SPICE is a family of circuit-simulation methods and tools that solve mathematical models of electronic components and networks.
A SPICE resistor is a simulation element defined by a reference, two nodes, and a resistance value.
A DC voltage source is a circuit or simulation element that maintains a specified voltage polarity between two nodes within its model assumptions.
Operating-point analysis calculates the steady-state DC voltages and currents of a circuit model before time-varying behavior is considered.
Logic Low is the digital simulator state representing the low logical value.
Logic High is the digital simulator state representing the high logical value.
Logic Unknown is the digital simulator state used when a valid high or low result cannot be determined from the available inputs and rules.
A digital event records a logic-state change or stimulus on a named net at a specified simulation time.
Propagation delay is the specified time between an input change and the resulting output change of a digital element.
Event-driven simulation advances a digital model by processing discrete scheduled state changes rather than continuously solving every point in time.
An electrical rule check examines schematic connectivity and typed-pin relationships for implemented topology errors or warnings without inventing missing electrical behavior.
A design rule check compares PCB geometry and assignments against implemented layout and fabrication constraints.
Visual-only accuracy means an asset can support appearance or interaction but lacks enough verified engineering data for electrical or fabrication claims.
Partial accuracy means some engineering properties or mappings are verified while other required information remains incomplete or unsupported.
Verified accuracy means the required data for the supported scope has passed the project's validation contract with revisioned supporting sources.
A fabrication export gate blocks manufacturing output when required geometry, mappings, sources, or validations are missing or invalid.
Engineering signoff is permission to treat a requirement as satisfied only after the required validated solver, data, and checks support that conclusion.
A canonical record is a deterministic serialized representation used to make validation inputs and outputs reproducible and comparable.
Solver input is validated structured data that is permitted to be passed to an engineering solver without claiming the solver's result in advance.
Measured-versus-modelled calibration compares simulation results with instrumented measurements while preserving fixture, environment, model, version, uncertainty, and timestamp provenance.
